content: Approach to Matching Dairy Foods Milk: In alignment with the U.S. food pattern modeling exercise, all fluid milk was matched to whole milk with 3.5% milk fat, as per the German food composition database. Yogurt and Fermented Milk Products: In the U.S. food pattern modeling exercise, all yogurts were matched to low-fat, unsweetened varieties. However, in the context of Optifood modeling, this approach could lead to the model selecting yogurt over fluid milk due to its ability to provide certain nutrients at a lower caloric cost (given that total calories are constrained). To address this, yogurts were matched to full-fat, unfortified varieties in both the U.S. and German food composition databases (e.g., regular and Greek-style full-fat yogurts). Buttermilk, being naturally low in fat, was matched accordingly. Cheese: Selecting appropriate food composition data for cheeses posed several challenges. Globally, there is a wide variety of cheeses, but intake datasets and food item lists often poorly describe them. Additionally, the U.S. food composition database does not consistently specify whether nutrient values for cheese reflect the use of fortified milk. This ambiguity made it difficult to determine nutrient values from the database. The German food composition database, which generally uses unfortified milk, provided generic items for hard, semi-hard, semi-soft, and soft cheeses. These were used when descriptions allowed. Specific cheeses in the U.S. SR28 database were matched when it was feasible to confirm they were unfortified. Approach to Matching Fish Matching fish accurately was the most challenging among all food groups due to the vast variety of fish species and the variability in nutrient content based on species and environmental factors. Common fish names in dietary intake datasets and food composition databases often refer to multiple species, adding to the complexity. Fish were matched where possible, but many could only be assigned to several unspecified codes. Approach to Matching Oils Cooking oils are often poorly described in dietary datasets and food item lists. Respondents frequently cannot specify the type of oil used or may only report a brand name. In cases where no information on oil types was available for a country’s food item list, data from the FAO was used to create a shortlist of cooking oils for that country. Oils accounting for at least 20% of the total food supply quantity (in kg/capita/year) were identified, typically yielding a list of one to three oils. These oils were substituted for unspecified oils when developing the nutrient profile for the subgroup other oils. Average Items Calculation of Average Items: Average items were calculated in two scenarios: 1. For each consumed item, nutrient values were averaged from multiple items in the source database. 2. For partially specified food items, nutrient values were averaged across similar items in the database. For example, maize (corn) items were averaged across various forms (e.g., whole grain, refined, yellow, white) using USDA SR28 data. When nutrient values for refined white maize flour were unavailable, values for yellow maize flour were used, with adjustments for vitamin A content. Meat: For commonly consumed types of meat, average nutrient values were derived across selected SR items. Wet-cooked items (e.g., boiled, stewed) were prioritized, as these are more typical for infant and young child (IYC) preparation. Lean items were selected based on fat content, with beef and ground beef defined as lean if containing less than 10% fat. For other meats, lean items were identified as those below the median fat content for the group. Generic Items and Missing Nutrient Values Generic Items: Generic items (e.g., unspecified cereals or unspecified vegetables) often lacked nutrient values. For some items, nutrient values were imputed from similar items in the database. For example, choline values were imputed from SR28 for unfortified items in the German database. Handling Missing Nutrient Data: Missing nutrient values were generally left as missing unless the subgroup had few items, and missing values would result in insufficient nutrient data for the subgroup. In such cases, imputations were made on a dry matter basis. For example, fatty acids and tryptophan were imputed for small fish using data from similar items in the Kenyan food composition database or SR28. Fortified and Unhealthy Food Items Fortified Items: Three types of fortified items were modeled: multiple-micronutrient powders (MNPs), small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS), and fortified infant cereals. Nutrient content for MNPs and SQ-LNS was based on specifications from UN agencies, while fortified infant cereals were modeled using a common food aid commodity, Super Cereal Plus. Unhealthy Foods: For unhealthy foods and beverages (e.g., sweetened drinks, biscuits, chips), nutrient profiles were created by averaging across selected items from databases such as USDA SR28 and the New Zealand food composition database. Missing values for certain nutrients (e.g., magnesium, copper, choline) were imputed from similar items.
